What Is an AI Acceptable Use Policy?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 2 October 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

An AI acceptable use policy is a short document that tells staff which AI tools they may use at work, what data they may and may not put into them, which uses need review or approval, and who to ask when unsure. It is the practical front end of AI governance. For a firm of 20 to 500 people, a one-page policy with a clear data rule and a named owner does more than a long one nobody reads.

What an AI acceptable use policy means

Acceptable use policies are familiar from IT: rules for email, devices and internet use. An AI version applies the same idea to tools that receive and process whatever staff give them. It answers the questions people actually have: can I use this, can I paste this into it, and do I need to tell anyone?

It is narrower than an AI governance programme. Governance covers inventories, risk assessment, vendor review and accountability. The acceptable use policy is the part every employee reads.

An AI acceptable use policy isIt is not
Rules for how staff use AI tools at workThe full AI governance programme
Short enough to read in five minutesA legal document only counsel understands
Specific about data classes and approved toolsA general statement of ethical principles
Owned, dated and reviewedA file written once and forgotten

Why it matters

Frameworks expect one

NIST's Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (AI 600-1, July 2024) includes the policy among its suggested governance actions. Action GV-1.4-002 calls for transparent acceptable use policies that address illegal use of generative AI. GV-3.2-003 calls for policies covering interfaces, modalities and human-AI configurations. GV-6.1-010 asks that they be updated to cover both proprietary and open-source tools.

The EU expects training on it

Article 4 of the EU AI Act sets an AI literacy duty for providers and deployers of AI systems. According to Covington's summary of the European Commission's May 2025 Q&A, it requires organisations to train anyone directly dealing with AI systems. The obligation has applied since 2 February 2025. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 softened it in July 2026 to a duty to take measures to support AI literacy, with no specific level required of any individual. The Commission's updated Q&A says national authorities supervise it from 2 August 2026 and no certificate is required. See What Is AI Literacy? for the amended text. There is no prescribed curriculum, but relying only on instructions for use may not be enough. A clear policy, with a record of who has been briefed on it, is a reasonable foundation.

Most firms have nothing written

IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach study, researched by the Ponemon Institute, found 63% of breached organisations had no AI governance policy or were still developing one. Gartner, reporting a survey of cybersecurity leaders in November 2025, put defining clear enterprise-wide policies for AI tool usage first among its recommendations against shadow AI.

The policy people read is the one that tells them, in a sentence, what they must never paste.

What to put in it

Eight sections cover most firms. Each should fit in a few lines.

SectionWhat it says
Purpose and ownerWhy the policy exists; the named person who maintains it
Approved toolsThe list, how to request access, how to request a new tool
Data rulesWhat may never be entered; what may be entered only into approved tools
Uses needing reviewClient-facing output, pricing, legal or HR content, anything sent externally
Prohibited usesIllegal uses, impersonation, recording without consent, decisions about people without review
Agents and automationNo agent may send, pay or delete without a named person approving
DisclosureWhen to tell clients or colleagues that AI was used
Incidents and reviewHow to report a mistake or leak; date of next review

A simple data rule

The data section carries most of the risk. A three-tier rule is easy to remember.

TierExamplesRule
NeverPasswords, payment card data, health data, data under a client NDA forbidding itNot into any AI tool
Approved tools onlyClient names, pricing, proposals, CRM exports, call recordingsOnly into tools on the approved list
OpenPublic information, generic drafting with no client detailAny tool, with judgment

Tie it to autonomy

For agents, the policy should say what level of autonomy is allowed without further approval. lowob's default is that nothing sends without a person: an agent may answer or draft, and may act with approval, but outbound messages, payments and deletions need a named approver. Writing that into the policy makes it a rule rather than a habit.

lowob takeaways

  • One page. A short policy that staff read beats a long one they skip.
  • Lead with data. Say exactly what must never be entered into any AI tool.
  • List the approved tools. A policy without an approved option drives use out of sight.
  • Own and date it. Name the owner, record who was briefed and review it at least twice a year.

Common questions

What should an AI acceptable use policy include?

The policy's owner, approved tools, data that must never be entered, uses that need review, prohibited uses, rules for agents, disclosure expectations and how to report incidents.

Do small businesses need an AI policy?

Any firm whose staff use AI tools with client or company data benefits from one. Without it, people make their own rules, and shadow AI follows.

Is an AI acceptable use policy required by law?

Not as such in most places. The EU AI Act requires AI literacy among relevant staff, and a written policy with briefing records is a common way to support that.

How often should an AI policy be updated?

At least twice a year, and whenever a new tool is approved, a major model changes or an incident occurs.
